analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from erasing lawsuits against companies and owners who never filed for bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: Introduced on July 30, 2024 with 6 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In big corporate bankruptcies, courts sometimes wipe out lawsuits that ordinary people hold against a company's owners or affiliates, even though those parties never filed for bankruptcy themselves. This bill would ban that practice unless the person holding the claim agrees in writing, limit temporary holds on those lawsuits to 90 days, and let judges throw out bankruptcies engineered to move assets away from liabilities. It died in committee without ever getting a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People and businesses holding legal claims that bankruptcy plans routinely extinguish — victims of defective products, opioid cases, financial misconduct, and other corporate wrongdoing. Their right to sue the people actually responsible would be protected, and they could not be punished or rewarded for refusing to go along with a release.

how_it_helps.text: Courts could no longer approve or order the discharge, release, or modification of a non-debtor's liability to someone else unless that person expressly consents in a signed writing — silence or inaction would not count, and a claimant's treatment under a plan could not depend on whether they consented [S2].

Temporary stays that block claimants from pursuing lawsuits against non-debtors would expire 90 days after the bankruptcy order unless the claimant agrees, and such stays could be appealed immediately [S2].

Courts would have to dismiss a Chapter 11 case if, within the past 10 years, the company was reshaped through a divisional merger that separated its assets from its liabilities and left the liabilities behind — the structure used to move litigation targets into bankruptcy while keeping healthy assets elsewhere [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, their owners, and affiliates facing mass-tort and other lawsuits would lose the ability to obtain court-ordered releases from those claims through a bankruptcy filing, leaving them exposed to litigation and potentially smaller, less coordinated settlements. Restructuring advisers would lose a key product they sell.

drawbacks.text: Coordinated bankruptcies can produce larger total payouts than scattered lawsuits: in the Purdue Pharma case, the Sackler family agreed to pay billions in exchange for a release, money that piece-by-piece litigation against their companies might never have recovered. A flat ban removes the tool that made such global settlements possible [S2] (general mechanism, widely reported).
The bill applies immediately to cases already pending when it takes effect, potentially unwinding restructurers' planning mid-case and adding years of litigation [S2].

Defenders of third-party releases argue they are sometimes necessary to complete a reorganization at all, since creditors and other parties may refuse to participate without settling their claims against affiliated parties [S2] (general mechanism).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core purpose — that no one should have their day in court erased without agreeing to it — directly protects people with legitimate claims, and its carve-outs (true consent in writing, no penalty for refusing, 90-day cap on stays) are carefully drawn. The honest trade-off is that some victims may receive less money in total when a coordinated global settlement is blocked and claims are pursued one lawsuit at a time against thinly capitalized entities. Weighing those, the bill's protections for claimants' consent are substantial and its costs fall on parties who created the liability in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler and five Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on July 30, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S2][S4].
Six of 216 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did [S3].
The action history shows only introduction and committee referral — no subcommittee action, markup, committee vote, or floor consideration — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, their owners, and the restructuring advisers who arrange bankruptcy deals that extinguish lawsuits against non-debtors — the practice the bill would have banned remains available, and the Supreme Court's narrower limits in the Purdue Pharma case do not reach consensual releases or other stay tactics.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies and owners facing mass-tort suits

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced and cosponsored only by Democrats (sponsor plus 6 of 216 House Democratic cosponsors) and received no recorded Republican support before the committee took no action on it [S1][S3][S4].

industries.industry: Bankruptcy restructuring firms and mass-tort defense counsel
industries.note: The bill outlaws the non-debtor release and the extended third-party stay, the tools restructuring advisers sell to companies and owners who want mass-tort claims resolved — and cut off — inside a bankruptcy filing. Claimants would keep their right to sue unless they choose to settle [S2].

industries.industry: Private equity firms and parent companies using divisional ('Texas two-step') restructurings
industries.note: The bill directs courts to dismiss bankruptcies filed within 10 years of a restructuring that split a company's assets from its liabilities, a strategy used to move litigation targets into bankruptcy while leaving healthy assets protected elsewhere. This removes a key shield for entities trying to ring-fence mass-tort liabilities [S2].

industries.industry: Owners and affiliates of companies facing large tort claims
industries.note: They could no longer obtain court-ordered releases of their personal or affiliate liability without each claimant's express written consent, meaning lawsuits against them survive bankruptcy plans [S2].
